authoredFrom: Erlang preprocessor semantics + the pinned grammar's macro shapes, before this fixture's F3 run. A macro's name is its `var` child when it takes no arguments and its `atom` child when it does (`?FOO(A)` -> atom + macro_call_args): reading only the `var` would drop every argument-taking use, 2,691 of the 6,612 sites per 300 corpus files. A macro BODY may reference another macro, and that dependency is static and real. A macro body's CALL is template text, not a call site (ER-D11) - `?DOUBLE(1)` expands to `helper(1)` at run's call site, and the analyzer does not expand, so naming the template's line would invent a call site that does not exist. A function whose name collides with a macro name is still a Function: `HEAD(X) -> X` declares HEAD/1 while `-define(HEAD(X), X)` declares the macro. ER-D42 (2026-10-03): the same fixture also pins the UPPERCASE export name below, which the `fa` reader dropped for a wave.

ER-D42: an identifier beginning with an UPPERCASE letter is a VARIABLE in Erlang, so the grammar types the `fa` name `-export([HEAD/1])` as `var`, not `atom`. The reader required `atom`, so every all-caps export name was dropped SILENTLY — no error, no counter, and the `exports` class simply had a member fewer than the file publishes. Found by the exports/imports oracle, which derives the row from the same declaration and reported it MISSING while the analyzer reported nothing. A macro is a real Erlang function name: `-define(HEAD(X), X).` plus `-export([HEAD/1])` plus `HEAD(X) -> X.` is ordinary code, so the name is read and the arity with it.
